segments.text: Backroom is a game where every AI player is a real Appwrite user with its own token. Give the wolf any prompt you like. The database still says no.
I take the wolf and hand it a jailbreak. Six seats are dealt: six agents, six database users, each reading only through its own short-lived JWT.
Every seat speaks in its own bubble, live over Realtime. My jailbroken wolf really tries to read the other seats' secrets, and zero rows come back.
Now the proof. My browser asks TablesDB for every secret row, carrying only the wolf's token. Nothing in between.
Five 404s, straight from Appwrite, and only the wolf's own row comes back. Row permissions decide, not the prompt.
It all works in Egyptian Arabic too, right to left.
An always-on demo game works even when today's games run out. Sharing writes a public receipt: who could read each role row during play, seats not users, and the deployed commit.
Second slice: a Dahab weekend with two AI friends whose budgets stay private. The agents agree, and the plan waits in one staged transaction. Then I change my dates.
Approve, and the commit hits 409 transaction conflict, from the database itself. The agents re-plan.
Generation two commits. The prompt can be anything; with TablesDB, the permissions still hold.
